title: I Will Always Love Dolly
author: Scott Yenor
content:
![I Will Always Love
Dolly](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/IMG_4380-1.jpg)

Dolly Parton, the last surviving [_First Lady of Country
Music_](https://claremontreviewofbooks.com/the-first-ladies-of-country-
music/?ref=compactmag.com), has died. Like the other first ladies Tammy
Wynette, Loretta Lynn and Patsy Cline, Dolly will forever be known by her
first name. She rose from obscurity (the fourth of twelve children) to reach
the heights of that most American genre.

Her big break came in 1967, when she won the audition to be the "girl singer"
on the Porter Wagoner Show. Dolly sang occasional duets with Wagoner, who was
then the bigger name. After several years playing second fiddle, Dolly had
success as a solo artist. Her early songs had strong lyrics and evoked a
polished version of the mountain music of her Tennessee home. Her first
country number one, the playful "Joshua"
([_1971_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFobROlmWxI&ref=compactmag.com)),
was an uptempo song about how an apparently mean, vicious man living alone in
a run down shack could warm up when exposed to the smile of a friendly woman.
Most country fans felt the same way about Dolly as Joshua did.

After Loretta's success singing about her upbringing in Kentucky's Butcher
Hollow in "Coal Miner's Daughter," Dolly penned a paean to a dying world of
homemade clothes and family Bible readings in "Coat of Many Colors" (1971).
Her mama sewed the jacket together from worn out rags. Some laughed at the
threadbare coat, but Dolly had learned to cherish the maternal love it
signified. Her 1973 album _Tennessee Mountain Home_ (1973) also pays tribute
to her home. The album's title celebrates the beauty of the hills and "walking
home from church on a Sunday with the one you love," while "In the Good Old
Days (When Times Were Bad)" makes clear that Dolly loved the lessons of
poverty, but didn't want to return to it. She would not be.

In danger of being typecast, Dolly decided to go solo. She told Wagoner
privately about her intentions by singing him "I Will Always Love You,"
arguably her most lasting, popular song. Dolly broached the topic of leaving
the show with Wagoner before, but he resisted. Dolly meant to convey her
gratitude for Wagoner, but also her need to go out on her own. At times the
song has an "It's not you, it's me" feel: "If I should stay/ I would only be
in your way." But the overall sense is deep appreciation and gratitude makes
this the classiest break-up song. Later adaptations, especially Whitney
Houston's even more famous cover from the early 1990s, grasp the great
subtlety of "Always Love You."

Porter agreed to her leaving if he could produce her next album. That album,
"Jolene" (1974), contains both the title track and "Always Love You." "Jolene"
marked Dolly's entry into the great country cheatin' song sweepstakes. Tammy
[_stood by
her_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AM-b8P1yj9w&ref=compactmag.com)
adulterous man. Loretta
[_threatened_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YgylOni0JSI&ref=compactmag.com)
and [_put
down_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GvxwMYPynnI&ref=compactmag.com) the
homewreckers for tempting her man. Dolly begs Jolene not to take her man,
though she understands why he might love Jolene (her beauty is beyond
compare). Eventually, modern country singers would settle on [_keying his
car_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WaSy8yy-mr8&ref=compactmag.com),
[_burning his
stuff_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rB7ONnfIjaI&ref=compactmag.com), or
[_killing
him_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oVEBZLrjpw4&ref=compactmag.com).

> "In these early hits, love was always a serious concern."

In these early hits, love was always a serious concern. It was central to
happiness and best embodied in marriage. It could be found in unexpected
places. The world today, in which men and women are suspicious of one another,
needs poets to help heal the breach. Dolly's "Bargain Store"
([_1975_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D1TXnTjbf4A&ref=compactmag.com)), a
song about a woman with a low reputation who promises to be a gem of a wife,
may be just such a song. The song's simple arrangement supports lyrics that
promise confession, forgiveness and healing: "My life is like unto a bargain
store/ And I may have just what you're looking for/ if you don't mind the fact
that all the merchandise is used/But with a little mending it could be as good
as new."

Later, Dolly would be a movie star. She would have a series of great cross
over hits starting in the late 1970s, including duets with Kenny Rogers, Ricky
Van Shelton, and Brad Paisley. She would operate a theme park, Dollywood. She
was the consummate entertainer. Her cheap wig and her trashy look are
themselves the [_stuff of
song_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NVUGCdTVpug&ref=compactmag.com). "It
costs a lot of money to look this cheap" would, she joked, probably be an
epitaph on her tombstone. Later in life she referred to her trademark breasts
as "shock and awe." Nothing, however, matches the beauty and depths of her old
American stories.

Dolly, by all appearances, was happily married in 1966. Her marriage of fifty-
nine years ended in 2025, when her husband, Carl Thomas Dean, died. According
to legend, Dean only watched her perform a few times in their long marriage.
He missed out. And now we will all miss out watching Dolly sing too. RIP.
